why.correct: Raising the pH removes nothing from salts whose ions do not react with OH⁻. Br⁻ and SO₄²⁻ are very weak bases and do not react with OH⁻ either. (Phosphate and carbonate salts become, if anything, less soluble as pH rises, because their anions stay unprotonated.)
options: Right: Br⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid.
Phosphate salts are strongly affected by pH: they dissolve in acid, and raising the pH reverses that.
Right: SO₄²⁻ is a very weak base, so its salts are hardly affected by pH.
Carbonate salts are strongly pH dependent.
Adding OH⁻ to a hydroxide salt is a common-ion effect: it lowers the solubility.

why.correct: Only basic anions (F⁻, CO₃²⁻, PO₄³⁻, OH⁻, S²⁻ and similar) react with H₃O⁺; that reaction is what shifts the dissolving equilibrium.
options: Right: the anion must be a base.
Salts of Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻ and NO₃⁻ are unaffected by pH.
Ksp does not change; Q does.
Anions from strong acids are unaffected by pH in either direction.
